chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from al-Husayn ibn Ishaq, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Durust, from one of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent two angels to the people of a city to overturn it upon its inhabitants. So when they arrived at the city, they found a man supplicating to Allah and pleading humbly. One of the angels said to his companion: 'Do you not see this supplicator?' He said: 'I have seen him, but I must proceed with what my Lord has commanded me.' He said: 'No, but I will not do anything until I refer it back to my Lord.' So he returned to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and said: 'O Lord, I arrived at the city and found Your servant so-and-so supplicating to You and pleading to You.' He said: 'Proceed with what I commanded you, for that man has never had his face clouded with anger towards Me at all.'
ai.seo_question: Why did the angels delay destroying the city when they saw a man praying?
ai.summary: In this narrative from *Al-Kafi*, two angels tasked with destroying a city pause to observe a devout servant deeply engaged in supplication, highlighting the power of *du'a* to potentially delay divine decree. God commands them to proceed, noting that the man’s face never showed anger towards Him, implying his piety was pure and not marred by resentment, thus justifying the decree despite his devotion. This reflects the Shia scholarly understanding of how individual righteousness interacts with collective destiny, where sincere worship is recognized even if it does not avert the ultimate judgment.
